samples.text:
These days, many people use the internet to do almost all their daily tasks, for example paying bills, buying food and contacting government offices. I think this is a positive development for most people, but it can cause problems for some groups.

The main advantage of doing things online is that it save a lot of time. In the past, people had to wait in long queue at the bank or at a government office, and sometimes they needed to take a day off work. Now they can transfer money or renew a document in few minutes from their home. This is very convenient, especially for people who is busy with work and family.

Another benefit is that online services are available all the time. Shops and offices close in the evening, but websites and apps are open 24 hours. People who live in villages far from the city can also use the same services as people in the city, so they do not need to travel.

On the other hand, not everyone is comfortable with technology. Many elderly people do not know how to use smartphones, and they may feel left behind when banks close their branches. In addition, there is a risk of online fraud. Some people lose their money because criminals steal their passwords or send fake emails.

In conclusion, I believe that doing everyday tasks online is mostly a positive development because it is fast and convenient for most people. However, the government and companies should still keep some offices open for people who cannot use internet, and they should teach people how to stay safe online.
samples.why: Clear overall position · relevant but fairly general ideas · simple, mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary with some repetition · frequent errors in agreement, articles and plurals that do not impede communication.

samples.text:
In many parts of the world, people now manage their finances, do their shopping and even apply for official documents without leaving home. In my view, this shift to online services is largely positive, although it must be managed carefully so that vulnerable groups are not excluded.

The clearest benefit is convenience. Tasks that once required a trip across town and a long wait in a queue can now be completed in minutes on a smartphone, at any time of day. For working parents or people with demanding jobs, this saves hours every month. It also benefits those living in rural areas, who previously had to travel long distances to reach a bank branch or a government office.

Online systems can also make services more efficient and transparent. When forms are submitted digitally, applications are processed faster and there are fewer opportunities for paperwork to be lost. In addition, digital records allow citizens to track the progress of a request, which reduce the frustration of not knowing what is happening. Governments and banks, meanwhile, can cut their running costs and, in theory, pass these savings on to the public.

Nevertheless, the move online has created real difficulties for some people. Older citizens and those on low incomes may lack the devices or skills needed to use digital services confidently, and as physical branches close, they risk being left without support. The growth of online fraud is another serious concern, since criminals increasingly target people who are unfamiliar with technology.

Overall, I believe the advantages of handling everyday tasks online outweigh the disadvantages, making this a positive development. However, it will only remain so if face-to-face options are kept for those who need them and people are taught how to protect themselves online.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · main ideas extended with relevant support · logical organisation and varied cohesion · good range of vocabulary (transparent, running costs) · mostly accurate grammar with an occasional slip.

samples.text:
Over the past two decades, the internet has quietly absorbed many of the routine chores of adult life. Bills are paid through banking apps, groceries arrive at the door and tax returns are filed on government portals. I consider this a broadly positive development, provided that it does not become compulsory for those unable to take part.

The most compelling argument in its favour is the time it returns to people. A task that might once have consumed an entire morning, involving a bus journey, a queue and a counter that closed at four o'clock, can now be completed during a lunch break. This flexibility is particularly valuable for shift workers, carers and residents of remote areas, for whom physical offices were always difficult to reach. In effect, digital services have removed a hidden tax on people's time.

There are systemic gains as well. Digital applications can be processed more quickly and consistently than paper ones, and the automatic record they create makes institutions more accountable. A citizen who can see exactly where a benefit claim has stalled is in a far stronger position than one waiting anxiously for a letter. Moreover, the savings from reduced administration can, at least in principle, be redirected towards improving the services themselves.

The danger lies in treating online access as universal when it is not. Many elderly people, as well as those who cannot afford reliable internet access, find digital systems bewildering, and the closure of branches can leave them dependent on relatives or simply unable to manage their own affairs. The rise of sophisticated online scams compounds this problem, as it is often the least confident users who are targeted.

In conclusion, the migration of everyday tasks online has made life markedly easier for the majority, and I therefore view it positively. Its benefits will only be fairly shared, however, if traditional channels remain available for those who still depend on them.
samples.why: Clear, qualified judgement fully developed · ideas extended with precise examples · confident paragraphing and cohesion · wide, flexible vocabulary (hidden tax, accountable, compounds) · wide range of structures with rare errors.
